title: AP Biology: Core Terms
description: For AP Biology students: original definitions and examples covering cellular chemistry, energy, heredity, evolution, and ecology. Built for concept recall and connections across units.

cards.back: The smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity.
cards.example: A carbon atom has six protons.

cards.back: One of several forms of an element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
cards.example: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes.

cards.back: A chemical bond formed by sharing electron pairs.
cards.example: Water contains covalent O-H bonds.

cards.back: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
cards.example: Sodium and chloride attract in a salt crystal.

cards.back: An attraction involving a partially positive hydrogen covalently bonded to an electronegative atom and another electronegative atom.
cards.example: Hydrogen bonds help stabilize DNA base pairing.

cards.back: An atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond.
cards.example: Oxygen attracts bonding electrons more strongly than hydrogen.

cards.back: Uneven charge distribution within a bond or molecule.
cards.example: Water has a partial negative charge near oxygen.

cards.back: Attraction among molecules of the same substance.
cards.example: Water molecules cohere in a droplet.

cards.back: Attraction between different substances.
cards.example: Water adheres to plant cell walls.

cards.back: Resistance of a liquid surface to expansion, arising from cohesive forces.
cards.example: Small insects can stand on water's surface.

cards.back: Heat required to raise the temperature of a unit mass by one degree.
cards.example: Water's high specific heat buffers temperature changes.

cards.back: A substance that donates protons in the Brønsted-Lowry model.
cards.example: Hydrochloric acid donates H+ in water.

cards.back: A substance that accepts protons in the Brønsted-Lowry model.
cards.example: Ammonia can accept H+ to form ammonium.

cards.back: A logarithmic measure of hydrogen ion activity, approximated by −log10[H+] in dilute solutions.
cards.example: A drop of one pH unit means about tenfold greater H+ concentration.

cards.back: A system that resists pH changes by accepting or releasing protons.
cards.example: Bicarbonate participates in blood buffering.

cards.back: A small building block that can be joined to form a polymer.
cards.example: An amino acid is a protein monomer.

cards.back: A large molecule composed of repeating or related monomer units.
cards.example: DNA is a nucleotide polymer.

cards.back: Formation of a covalent linkage accompanied by removal of water components.
cards.example: Two sugar units can join through a condensation reaction.

cards.back: Cleavage of a chemical bond through addition of water components.
cards.example: Digestive enzymes hydrolyze many food polymers.

cards.back: A class of molecules including sugars and their polymers, used in energy storage and structure.
cards.example: Starch stores glucose units in plants.

cards.back: A single sugar unit that cannot be hydrolyzed into simpler carbohydrates.
cards.example: Glucose is a monosaccharide.

cards.back: A carbohydrate made of two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond.
cards.example: Sucrose contains glucose and fructose.

cards.back: A polymer of many sugar units.
cards.example: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide.

cards.back: A plant glucose-storage polysaccharide with alpha glycosidic linkages.
cards.example: Potato tubers contain starch.

cards.back: A highly branched glucose-storage polysaccharide found in animals and many fungi.
cards.example: Liver cells store glycogen.

cards.back: A structural polymer of glucose with beta-1,4 linkages in plant cell walls.
cards.example: Cellulose microfibrils help support stems.

cards.back: A structural polysaccharide containing nitrogen-bearing sugar units.
cards.example: Fungal cell walls contain chitin.

cards.back: A largely hydrophobic or amphipathic biomolecule, including fats, phospholipids, and steroids.
cards.example: Membranes contain phospholipids.

cards.back: A fat molecule consisting of glycerol esterified to three fatty acids.
cards.example: Adipose tissue stores triglycerides.

cards.front: What is a saturated fatty acid?
cards.back: A fatty acid with no carbon-carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.
cards.example: Saturated chains can pack closely together.

cards.front: What is an unsaturated fatty acid?
cards.back: A fatty acid with at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
cards.example: A cis double bond creates a bend in the chain.

cards.back: An amphipathic lipid with a phosphate-containing polar region and hydrophobic tails.
cards.example: Phospholipids self-assemble into bilayers.

cards.back: A lipid characterized by four fused carbon rings.
cards.example: Cholesterol is a steroid.

cards.back: An organic molecule with amino and carboxyl groups; protein amino acids also have a characteristic side chain.
cards.example: Glycine has hydrogen as its side chain.

cards.back: The covalent linkage between one amino acid's carboxyl carbon and another's amino nitrogen.
cards.example: Peptide bonds join a polypeptide backbone.

cards.back: The linear amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
cards.example: Changing one residue changes primary structure.

cards.back: Local backbone folding patterns stabilized largely by backbone hydrogen bonds.
cards.example: Alpha helices and beta sheets are secondary structures.

cards.back: The overall three-dimensional conformation of one polypeptide chain.
cards.example: A globular enzyme has a folded tertiary structure.

cards.back: The arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits in a functional protein.
cards.example: Hemoglobin contains four subunits.

cards.back: Loss of normal protein conformation, often reducing function without breaking the peptide backbone.
cards.example: High heat can denature an enzyme.

cards.back: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that accelerates a reaction without being consumed overall.
cards.example: Amylase catalyzes starch breakdown.

cards.back: The enzyme region where substrates bind and catalysis occurs.
cards.example: A substrate's shape and chemistry affect active-site binding.

cards.back: A reactant acted on by an enzyme.
cards.example: Lactose is a substrate for lactase.

cards.back: The energy barrier that reactants must overcome to reach a transition state.
cards.example: Enzymes lower activation energy.

cards.back: Inhibition in which an inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site.
cards.example: More substrate can reduce the relative effect of an ideal competitive inhibitor.

cards.back: A change in protein activity caused by binding at a site distinct from the active site.
cards.example: A regulatory molecule can stabilize an inactive enzyme shape.

cards.back: Regulation in which a pathway's product inhibits an earlier step.
cards.example: An amino acid can inhibit its own synthesis pathway.

cards.back: A nonprotein component required for the activity of some enzymes.
cards.example: A bound metal ion may support catalysis.

cards.back: An organic cofactor that assists enzyme activity.
cards.example: NAD+ carries electrons between reactions.

cards.back: A molecule containing a nitrogenous base, a sugar, and one or more phosphate groups.
cards.example: ATP is a nucleotide.

cards.back: Deoxyribonucleic acid, a polymer that stores hereditary information in most organisms.
cards.example: A chromosome contains a long DNA molecule.

cards.back: Ribonucleic acid, a polymer involved in gene expression, regulation, and sometimes catalysis.
cards.example: Messenger RNA carries coding information to ribosomes.

cards.back: The opposite 5′-to-3′ orientations of the two strands in a DNA double helix.
cards.example: One strand runs 5′ to 3′ alongside a 3′ to 5′ partner.

cards.back: Specific pairing of bases through hydrogen bonding and compatible geometry.
cards.example: DNA pairs A with T and G with C.

cards.back: Adenosine triphosphate, a nucleotide whose hydrolysis can be coupled to energy-requiring processes.
cards.example: ATP powers many active transport pumps.

cards.back: A cell lacking a membrane-bound nucleus and the typical membrane-bound organelles of eukaryotes.
cards.example: Bacteria are prokaryotic organisms.

cards.back: A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound compartments.
cards.example: A plant leaf cell is eukaryotic.

cards.back: A selectively permeable boundary consisting mainly of a lipid bilayer and associated proteins.
cards.example: The membrane helps regulate ion movement.

cards.front: What is the fluid mosaic model?
cards.back: A model describing membranes as dynamic lipid bilayers containing diverse proteins and other components.
cards.example: Many membrane proteins move laterally.

cards.front: What is a selectively permeable membrane?
cards.back: A membrane that allows some substances to pass more readily than others.
cards.example: Small nonpolar molecules cross lipid bilayers relatively easily.

cards.back: The aqueous intracellular fluid outside membrane-bound organelles in a eukaryotic cell.
cards.example: Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.

cards.back: The eukaryotic organelle that encloses most cellular DNA.
cards.example: Transcription occurs in the nucleus of a typical animal cell.

cards.back: A nuclear region where ribosomal RNA is produced and ribosomal subunits begin assembly.
cards.example: An active nucleolus supports ribosome production.

cards.back: An RNA-protein complex that translates mRNA into a polypeptide.
cards.example: Free ribosomes make many cytosolic proteins.

cards.back: A membrane network bearing ribosomes that makes many secreted and membrane proteins.
cards.example: A secreted enzyme enters the rough ER during synthesis.

cards.back: An ER region involved in lipid synthesis, detoxification, or calcium storage, depending on the cell.
cards.example: Muscle smooth ER stores calcium.

cards.back: A membrane system that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids.
cards.example: Golgi vesicles can deliver cargo toward the cell surface.

cards.back: An acidic membrane-bound compartment containing hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion.
cards.example: Lysosomes digest material taken up by some animal cells.

cards.back: An organelle involved in oxidative reactions and management of hydrogen peroxide.
cards.example: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide in peroxisomes.

cards.back: A membrane-bound compartment for storage, digestion, or water balance.
cards.example: A plant's central vacuole contributes to turgor.

cards.back: An organelle that performs key stages of aerobic respiration and produces much cellular ATP.
cards.example: The inner membrane supports an electron transport chain.

cards.back: A photosynthetic organelle of plants and many algae.
cards.example: Chloroplast thylakoids contain chlorophyll.

cards.back: The explanation that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria engulfed by ancestral cells.
cards.example: Their own DNA and bacterial-like ribosomes support this origin.

cards.back: A network of protein filaments supporting cell shape, organization, and movement.
cards.example: Microtubules form the mitotic spindle.

cards.back: A hollow cytoskeletal polymer built from tubulin dimers.
cards.example: Microtubules guide chromosome movement.

cards.back: A thin cytoskeletal filament made of actin.
cards.example: Actin helps form the contractile ring in animal cytokinesis.

cards.back: A durable cytoskeletal fiber that provides mechanical support.
cards.example: Keratins help animal cells resist stress.

cards.back: A major microtubule-organizing center in many animal cells.
cards.example: Duplicated centrosomes contribute to spindle poles.

cards.back: A short cell-surface projection with a microtubule core, used in movement or sensing.
cards.example: Motile airway cilia move mucus.

cards.back: A long microtubule-based cell projection used for movement.
cards.example: A sperm cell swims using a flagellum.

cards.back: A rigid layer outside the plasma membrane that provides support and protection.
cards.example: Plant cell walls contain cellulose.

cards.back: A network of molecules outside animal cells that supports tissues and influences signaling.
cards.example: Collagen provides tensile strength in many tissues.

cards.back: An animal-cell junction that limits leakage between adjacent cells.
cards.example: Tight junctions help seal an intestinal epithelium.

cards.back: A channel connection permitting small molecules and ions to move between animal cells.
cards.example: Gap junctions support electrical coupling in heart muscle.

cards.back: A membrane-lined channel linking the cytoplasm of neighboring plant cells.
cards.example: Plasmodesmata allow intercellular transport.

cards.back: Net movement down a concentration gradient due to random molecular motion.
cards.example: Oxygen diffuses into a cell with lower oxygen concentration.

cards.back: Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane driven by water potential differences.
cards.example: Water enters a cell placed in a suitably hypotonic solution.

cards.back: Passive movement down an electrochemical gradient through membrane proteins.
cards.example: A channel allows ions to move down their gradient.

cards.back: Membrane transport against an electrochemical gradient, requiring an energy source.
cards.example: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP.

cards.back: The combined concentration and electrical forces affecting an ion's movement.
cards.example: A proton gradient can drive ATP synthesis.

cards.back: Membrane channels that increase water permeability.
cards.example: Aquaporins speed osmotic water movement.

cards.back: A solution with a lower effective concentration of nonpenetrating solutes than the comparison compartment.
cards.example: An animal cell may swell in a hypotonic environment.

cards.back: A solution with a higher effective concentration of nonpenetrating solutes than the comparison compartment.
cards.example: An animal cell may shrink in a hypertonic environment.

cards.back: A solution producing no sustained net osmotic volume change relative to the comparison cell.
cards.example: A cell retains approximately constant volume in an isotonic medium.

cards.back: Pressure of a plant cell's contents against its wall following water uptake.
cards.example: Turgor helps keep herbaceous stems upright.

cards.back: Separation of the plasma membrane from the wall as a plant cell loses water.
cards.example: A strongly hypertonic solution can cause plasmolysis.

cards.back: Uptake of extracellular material by inward budding of the plasma membrane.
cards.example: A cell can internalize receptor-bound cargo.

cards.back: Release of vesicle contents when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.
cards.example: A secretory cell releases proteins by exocytosis.

cards.back: Endocytosis of large particles or cells.
cards.example: A macrophage can engulf a bacterium.

cards.back: Selective uptake triggered by cargo binding to membrane receptors.
cards.example: Cells internalize LDL particles through receptors.

cards.back: The total set of chemical reactions in an organism.
cards.example: Metabolism includes synthesis and breakdown pathways.

cards.back: Metabolic reactions that break down molecules, often releasing usable energy.
cards.example: Glucose oxidation is catabolic.

cards.back: Metabolic reactions that build molecules and require energy input.
cards.example: Protein synthesis is anabolic.

cards.front: What is Gibbs free energy change?
cards.back: A measure predicting thermodynamic favorability at constant temperature and pressure; negative ΔG favors the forward process.
cards.example: ATP hydrolysis has a negative ΔG under typical cellular conditions.

cards.back: A reaction with negative Gibbs free energy change under the stated conditions.
cards.example: An exergonic reaction can supply energy for coupled work.

cards.back: A reaction with positive Gibbs free energy change under the stated conditions.
cards.example: Building a polymer often requires energy coupling.

cards.back: Using an energetically favorable process to drive an unfavorable one.
cards.example: ATP hydrolysis can drive phosphorylation of a substrate.

cards.back: Loss of electrons, often associated with loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen in biology.
cards.example: NADH is oxidized to NAD+ when it donates electrons.

cards.back: Gain of electrons.
cards.example: NAD+ is reduced when it accepts electrons and hydrogen.

cards.back: A set of pathways that extracts energy from fuel molecules and transfers some of it to ATP.
cards.example: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

cards.back: A cytosolic pathway converting one glucose into two pyruvate with a net gain of two ATP and two NADH.
cards.example: Glycolysis can proceed without directly using oxygen.

cards.back: Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, producing CO2 and NADH.
cards.example: In eukaryotes this occurs mainly in the mitochondrial matrix.

cards.front: What is the citric acid cycle?
cards.back: A cycle oxidizing acetyl groups to CO2 while producing reduced electron carriers and ATP or GTP.
cards.example: Oxaloacetate is regenerated each turn.

cards.back: ATP or GTP formation by direct transfer of a phosphate group from an organic intermediate.
cards.example: Some glycolytic steps make ATP this way.

cards.back: ATP production driven by electron transport and chemiosmosis during respiration.
cards.example: A mitochondrial proton gradient powers ATP synthase.

cards.front: What is an electron transport chain?
cards.back: A series of carriers that transfer electrons through redox reactions, often coupled to proton movement.
cards.example: Respiratory electrons ultimately reach oxygen in aerobic cells.

cards.back: Use of an electrochemical ion gradient to drive a process such as ATP synthesis.
cards.example: Protons flowing through ATP synthase help make ATP.
cards.hint: Connect an ion gradient to cellular work.

cards.back: A membrane enzyme complex that couples ion flow to ATP formation, and can operate in reverse.
cards.example: Chloroplast ATP synthase uses a proton gradient.

cards.back: A process that regenerates NAD+ by transferring electrons from NADH to an organic acceptor without a respiratory electron transport chain.
cards.example: Lactate fermentation permits continued glycolysis.

cards.back: Fermentation producing ethanol and CO2 while regenerating NAD+.
cards.example: Yeast releases CO2 during bread making.

cards.back: Reduction of pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+.
cards.example: Some cells increase lactate production when oxidative capacity is limited.

cards.back: Conversion of light energy into chemical energy, with carbon fixation in plants, algae, and some bacteria.
cards.example: Plants use light to support carbohydrate production from CO2.

cards.back: A pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
cards.example: Chlorophyll a participates in photosystem reaction centers.

cards.back: A pigment-protein complex that captures light and initiates electron transfer.
cards.example: Photosystem II can supply electrons from water.

cards.back: An internal chloroplast membrane sac containing photosynthetic electron-transfer machinery.
cards.example: Protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen during light reactions.

cards.back: The fluid compartment of a chloroplast outside the thylakoids.
cards.example: The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma.

cards.back: Photosynthetic reactions that use light to generate ATP and reducing power; oxygenic forms also release O2 from water.
cards.example: Linear electron flow produces NADPH.

cards.back: Light-supported splitting of water at photosystem II, providing electrons and releasing protons and oxygen.
cards.example: Photosynthetic oxygen originates from water.

cards.back: A cycle using ATP and NADPH to reduce fixed carbon and regenerate RuBP.
cards.example: Its net carbon product is triose phosphate.

cards.back: Incorporation of inorganic carbon into organic molecules.
cards.example: Rubisco attaches CO2 to RuBP.

cards.back: The enzyme that catalyzes carboxylation or oxygenation of RuBP.
cards.example: Rubisco initiates carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle.

cards.back: A pathway following Rubisco's oxygenation reaction that consumes resources and releases previously fixed carbon.
cards.example: Hot, dry conditions can favor photorespiration in C3 plants.

cards.back: A strategy that initially fixes carbon into four-carbon compounds and concentrates CO2 near Rubisco, often by spatial separation.
cards.example: Maize uses C4 photosynthesis.

cards.back: A strategy that generally fixes CO2 at night and uses stored carbon during the day, separating steps in time.
cards.example: Many cacti use CAM to conserve water.

cards.front: What is a signal transduction pathway?
cards.back: A sequence converting reception of a signal into a cellular response.
cards.example: Receptor activation can trigger a kinase cascade.

cards.back: A molecule that binds specifically to another molecule, often a receptor.
cards.example: A signaling molecule can be a receptor ligand.

cards.back: A protein that detects a signal through binding and initiates a response.
cards.example: A membrane receptor detects an extracellular ligand.

cards.back: A small intracellular molecule or ion that relays a signal from an activated receptor.
cards.example: Cyclic AMP can function as a second messenger.

cards.back: An enzyme that transfers a phosphate group, usually from ATP, to a protein.
cards.example: A kinase can activate another signaling protein.

cards.back: An enzyme that removes phosphate groups from proteins.
cards.example: A phosphatase can reverse a kinase's modification.

cards.back: An increase in the number of activated molecules as a signal passes through a pathway.
cards.example: One activated enzyme can modify many substrates.

cards.back: Regulated cell death involving an organized cellular dismantling process.
cards.example: Apoptosis helps remove certain damaged cells.

cards.back: A control mechanism in which a response opposes the initial change.
cards.example: Rising body temperature can trigger cooling responses.

cards.back: A control mechanism in which a response reinforces the initial change.
cards.example: Ethylene can promote further ethylene production during fruit ripening.

cards.back: Maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions through regulation.
cards.example: Cells regulate internal pH despite external changes.

cards.back: The sequence of cell growth, DNA replication, and division.
cards.example: A dividing eukaryotic cell progresses through G1, S, G2, and M phases.

cards.back: The G1, S, and G2 portions of the cell cycle between mitotic divisions.
cards.example: DNA replication takes place during interphase.

cards.back: The cell-cycle phase in which nuclear DNA is replicated.
cards.example: Each chromosome gains a sister chromatid during S phase.

cards.back: A regulatory control that can delay progression until conditions are suitable.
cards.example: A checkpoint can stop division after DNA damage.

cards.back: Proteins whose regulated abundance helps control cell-cycle transitions through cyclin-dependent kinases.
cards.example: Cyclin accumulation can activate a cell-cycle kinase.

cards.back: Division of a eukaryotic nucleus into two nuclei with corresponding chromosome sets.
cards.example: Mitosis supports growth of a multicellular organism.

cards.back: Division of the cytoplasm to form separate daughter cells.
cards.example: An animal cell's cleavage furrow forms during cytokinesis.

cards.back: A DNA molecule with associated proteins that carries genetic information.
cards.example: A replicated eukaryotic chromosome contains two sister chromatids.

cards.back: DNA and its associated proteins in a cell.
cards.example: Histones help package eukaryotic chromatin.

cards.back: A segment of DNA wrapped around a histone protein core.
cards.example: Nucleosomes organize eukaryotic chromosomes.

cards.back: The two replicated copies of a chromosome joined before separation.
cards.example: Sister chromatids separate during mitotic anaphase.

cards.back: A chromosome region that organizes kinetochore assembly and links sister chromatids before separation.
cards.example: Spindle microtubules attach through centromere-associated kinetochores.

cards.back: A protein complex assembled at a centromere that interacts with spindle microtubules.
cards.example: Kinetochores help move chromosomes.

cards.back: Chromosomes with corresponding gene loci, typically one inherited from each parent.
cards.example: A homologous pair can carry different alleles.

cards.back: A cell with two chromosome sets.
cards.example: Most human somatic cells are diploid.

cards.back: A cell with one chromosome set.
cards.example: A human sperm cell is haploid.

cards.back: A division process that follows one DNA replication with two nuclear divisions, usually producing haploid cells.
cards.example: Meiosis reduces chromosome-set number in sexual life cycles.

cards.back: Pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
cards.example: Synapsis brings homologous regions together.

cards.back: Exchange of corresponding DNA segments between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
cards.example: Crossing over creates new allele combinations.

cards.back: A visible connection between homologous chromosomes associated with a crossover.
cards.example: Chiasmata help hold homologs together before anaphase I.

cards.back: Independent segregation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis, producing varied combinations.
cards.example: Unlinked genes can follow independent assortment.

cards.back: Fusion of haploid gametes to form a zygote.
cards.example: Fertilization restores diploidy in the human life cycle.

cards.back: A DNA sequence whose expression contributes to a functional RNA or protein product.
cards.example: A gene may encode an enzyme.

cards.back: An alternative sequence form at a genetic locus.
cards.example: A population can contain several alleles of one gene.

cards.back: A physical location on a chromosome.
cards.example: Two alleles of a gene occupy corresponding loci on homologs.

cards.back: The allele composition of an organism at one or more loci.
cards.example: Aa is a heterozygous genotype.
cards.hint: Think of alleles rather than an observed trait.

cards.back: An observable characteristic influenced by genotype and environment.
cards.example: Flower color is a phenotype.

cards.back: Having two matching alleles at a locus in a diploid organism.
cards.example: AA is homozygous at the modeled locus.

cards.back: Having two different alleles at a locus in a diploid organism.
cards.example: Aa is heterozygous at the modeled locus.

cards.back: An allele whose associated phenotype appears in a heterozygote under a specified inheritance model.
cards.example: Complete dominance can make Aa resemble AA.

cards.back: An allele whose associated phenotype is masked in a heterozygote under complete dominance.
cards.example: The modeled recessive phenotype appears in aa.

cards.front: What is the law of segregation?
cards.back: The two alleles at a diploid locus separate during gamete formation, so a gamete typically receives one.
cards.example: An Aa individual can produce A or a gametes.

cards.back: A cross with a homozygous recessive individual used to investigate an unknown genotype.
cards.example: Recessive offspring can reveal heterozygosity in the tested parent.

cards.back: Inheritance in which the heterozygote phenotype is intermediate between the two homozygotes.
cards.example: Some red and white flower alleles produce pink heterozygotes.

cards.back: Inheritance in which both allelic products are detectably expressed in a heterozygote.
cards.example: AB blood type expresses both A and B antigens.

cards.back: The presence of more than two allelic forms at a locus in a population.
cards.example: The ABO system includes A, B, and O allelic classes.

cards.back: An effect in which one gene influences multiple traits.
cards.example: A pigment-related gene may affect more than one tissue.

cards.back: Inheritance in which variation at multiple genes contributes to a trait.
cards.example: Human height has many genetic contributors.

cards.back: An interaction in which one gene modifies or masks the effect of another gene.
cards.example: A pigment-production gene can mask a pigment-color gene.

cards.back: The tendency of nearby loci on the same chromosome to be inherited together.
cards.example: Closely spaced genes recombine less often than distant ones.

cards.back: The proportion of recombinant offspring or gametes in a genetic analysis.
cards.example: A 5% frequency suggests about 5 map units for nearby loci.

cards.back: A gene located on a sex chromosome.
cards.example: An X-linked gene can show different inheritance patterns in XX and XY individuals.

cards.back: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate normally.
cards.example: Meiotic nondisjunction can produce gametes with extra chromosomes.

cards.back: An abnormal number of particular chromosomes rather than whole chromosome sets.
cards.example: Trisomy is one form of aneuploidy.

cards.back: Possession of more than two complete chromosome sets.
cards.example: Many crop plants are polyploid.

cards.back: DNA replication in which each daughter duplex contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
cards.example: Each original strand serves as a template.

cards.back: An enzyme that separates the DNA strands during replication.
cards.example: Helicase opens a replication fork.

cards.back: An enzyme that extends DNA by adding nucleotides to a free 3′ end using a template.
cards.example: New DNA is synthesized 5′ to 3′.

cards.back: An enzyme that synthesizes short RNA primers for DNA replication.
cards.example: Primase supplies a starting 3′ end for DNA polymerase.

cards.back: The new DNA strand synthesized continuously toward an advancing replication fork.
cards.example: Leading-strand synthesis follows fork opening.

cards.back: The new DNA strand synthesized discontinuously away from an advancing replication fork.
cards.example: Its Okazaki fragments are later joined.

cards.back: A short DNA segment made during lagging-strand replication.
cards.example: DNA ligase helps connect adjacent fragments.

cards.back: An enzyme that seals breaks in a DNA sugar-phosphate backbone.
cards.example: Ligase joins processed Okazaki fragments.

cards.back: A protective repetitive DNA region at a linear chromosome's end.
cards.example: Telomeres help distinguish chromosome ends from DNA breaks.

cards.back: An enzyme complex that extends telomeric DNA using an internal RNA template.
cards.example: Telomerase is active in some stem and germ-line cells.

cards.back: A change in genetic sequence.
cards.example: A nucleotide substitution can alter a codon.

cards.back: A genetic change involving a single nucleotide position.
cards.example: One base pair can be replaced by another.

cards.back: A coding-sequence change that does not change the encoded amino acid.
cards.example: Different codons can specify the same amino acid.

cards.back: A coding change that substitutes one amino acid for another.
cards.example: A changed codon can replace a charged residue with a nonpolar one.

cards.back: A coding change that creates a premature stop codon.
cards.example: Translation may end before the usual protein length.

cards.back: An insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame, usually because its length is not a multiple of three.
cards.example: Deleting one coding nucleotide changes downstream codon grouping.

cards.back: Synthesis of RNA from a DNA template.
cards.example: RNA polymerase produces a primary transcript.

cards.back: An enzyme that builds RNA by reading a DNA template.
cards.example: It extends RNA in the 5′-to-3′ direction.

cards.back: A DNA region where transcription machinery assembles to begin transcription.
cards.example: Promoter sequence affects transcription initiation.

cards.back: A protein that helps regulate transcription by interacting with DNA or transcription machinery.
cards.example: Some transcription factors bind enhancers.

cards.back: A regulatory DNA sequence that can increase transcription through bound proteins.
cards.example: An enhancer may act far from its target promoter.

cards.back: Removal of introns and joining of exons in a transcript.
cards.example: A spliceosome processes many eukaryotic pre-mRNAs.

cards.back: A transcribed sequence removed during RNA splicing.
cards.example: An intron does not remain in the mature spliced mRNA.

cards.back: A transcript segment retained after splicing.
cards.example: An exon may include coding sequence or untranslated sequence.

cards.back: Production of different mature RNAs by joining exons in different combinations.
cards.example: One gene can contribute to multiple protein isoforms.

cards.back: Synthesis of a polypeptide using an mRNA sequence.
cards.example: A ribosome reads mRNA codons.

cards.back: A three-nucleotide mRNA sequence specifying an amino acid or a stop signal.
cards.example: AUG usually serves as the start codon.

cards.back: A three-nucleotide tRNA sequence that pairs with an mRNA codon.
cards.example: Complementarity helps match tRNA to the correct codon.

cards.back: An RNA adaptor that links codon recognition with delivery of an amino acid.
cards.example: An aminoacyl-tRNA carries an attached amino acid.

cards.back: The mapping of mRNA codons to amino acids and termination signals.
cards.example: Several codons can specify leucine.

cards.back: A group of genes transcribed together from shared regulatory control, common in prokaryotes.
cards.example: The lac operon coordinates lactose-use genes.

cards.back: A regulatory protein that reduces gene expression, often by binding DNA.
cards.example: A repressor can block transcription initiation.

cards.back: An operon whose expression rises in response to an inducing signal.
cards.example: The lac system is induced when lactose-related signals permit expression.

cards.back: An operon whose expression falls in response to a regulatory signal.
cards.example: Tryptophan can help repress the trp operon.

cards.back: Regulation associated with chromatin or other stable cellular states without changing the underlying DNA sequence.
cards.example: DNA methylation can influence gene expression.

cards.back: Sequence-specific gene silencing guided by small RNAs.
cards.example: A small RNA can guide degradation of a complementary transcript.

cards.back: An independently replicating DNA molecule distinct from a cell's main chromosome, often circular in bacteria.
cards.example: A bacterial plasmid may carry a resistance gene.

cards.back: An enzyme that cuts DNA at or near particular recognition sequences.
cards.example: A restriction enzyme can generate defined DNA fragments.

cards.back: A method that amplifies a selected DNA region through repeated temperature cycles and DNA synthesis.
cards.example: PCR uses primers flanking the target sequence.

cards.back: Separation of charged molecules through a gel in an electric field.
cards.example: Smaller DNA fragments generally migrate farther in an agarose gel.

cards.back: Determination of the nucleotide order in a DNA molecule.
cards.example: Sequencing can identify a substitution in a gene.

cards.back: A method using guide RNA and a Cas protein to target DNA for modification.
cards.example: A guide RNA can direct a nuclease to a chosen sequence.

cards.back: An acellular infectious entity with a genome that depends on host cells for reproduction.
cards.example: A bacteriophage infects bacteria.

cards.back: The protein shell surrounding a viral genome.
cards.example: Capsid proteins protect the packaged genome.

cards.back: A viral reproductive pathway that makes progeny and ends in host-cell lysis in the classic phage model.
cards.example: A lytic phage releases new particles when the bacterium bursts.

cards.back: A state in which a phage genome persists in a host without immediate lysis, often integrated into host DNA.
cards.example: An integrated prophage can later enter a lytic cycle.

cards.back: An enzyme that synthesizes DNA from an RNA template.
cards.example: Retroviruses use reverse transcription.

cards.back: Differential reproductive success associated with heritable variation in a particular environment.
cards.example: A heritable trait can increase when it improves reproductive success.

cards.back: Relative contribution of viable, reproducing offspring to subsequent generations.
cards.example: Survival matters evolutionarily when it contributes to reproduction.

cards.back: A heritable feature shaped by selection that improves performance in a particular environment.
cards.example: Camouflage can reduce detection by predators.

cards.back: Change in heritable characteristics of populations across generations.
cards.example: Allele frequencies can change over time.

cards.back: Individuals of the same species living in an area and potentially interacting and reproducing.
cards.example: Frogs breeding in one pond form a local population.

cards.back: All alleles present in a population.
cards.example: Migration can add alleles to a gene pool.

cards.back: The fraction of gene copies at a locus represented by a particular allele.
cards.example: If 20 of 100 copies are A, its frequency is 0.20.

cards.back: Random change in allele frequencies due to finite sampling across generations.
cards.example: Drift is especially strong in small populations.
cards.hint: Chance, rather than a consistent fitness advantage.

cards.back: Genetic drift associated with a sharp reduction in population size.
cards.example: A disaster can leave a genetically unrepresentative set of survivors.

cards.back: Genetic drift when a new population begins from a small sample of a larger one.
cards.example: A few colonists may carry unusual allele frequencies.

cards.back: Transfer of alleles among populations through migration and reproduction or gamete movement.
cards.example: Windborne pollen can move alleles between plant populations.

cards.back: A null model in which allele and genotype frequencies remain stable under specified assumptions.
cards.example: For two alleles, expected genotype frequencies are p², 2pq, and q².

cards.back: Selection favoring one end of a phenotypic distribution.
cards.example: A changing environment may favor larger average beak size.

cards.back: Selection favoring intermediate phenotypes relative to extremes.
cards.example: Intermediate trait values can yield the highest reproductive success.

cards.back: Selection favoring both extremes over intermediate phenotypes.
cards.example: Two distinct food sizes can favor two different beak sizes.

cards.back: Selection arising from differences in mating success.
cards.example: Mate preferences can favor elaborate displays.

cards.back: Human-directed differential reproduction for desired heritable traits.
cards.example: Selective breeding changes crop characteristics.

cards.front: What is a species under the biological species concept?
cards.back: A group of natural populations whose members can interbreed and are reproductively isolated from other such groups.
cards.example: The concept is difficult to apply to fossils and asexual organisms.

cards.back: Barriers that prevent gene flow between populations through successful reproduction.
cards.example: Different mating times can reduce interbreeding.

cards.back: A reproductive barrier acting before zygote formation.
cards.example: Incompatible mating behaviors can prevent mating.

cards.back: A reproductive barrier acting after fertilization.
cards.example: Hybrid sterility reduces gene flow.

cards.back: Speciation associated with geographic separation that restricts gene flow.
cards.example: A new physical barrier can divide a population.

cards.back: Speciation without geographic separation of the diverging populations.
cards.example: Polyploidy can initiate reproductive isolation in plants.

cards.back: Diversification of a lineage into forms occupying different ecological roles.
cards.example: Descendant species may specialize on different food sources.

cards.back: Structures sharing an evolutionary origin, even if their functions differ.
cards.example: Tetrapod forelimbs share underlying skeletal patterns.

cards.back: Structures with similar functions that evolved independently in the compared lineages.
cards.example: Bird and insect wings are analogous as flight structures.

cards.back: A reduced or modified inherited feature with diminished ancestral function, though it may retain other roles.
cards.example: Some cave animals retain reduced eyes.

cards.back: Independent evolution of similar traits in different lineages facing similar challenges.
cards.example: Streamlined bodies evolved in several aquatic lineages.

cards.back: An evolutionary history or a representation of relationships among lineages.
cards.example: A phylogenetic tree proposes common ancestry.

cards.back: An ancestor and all of its descendants.
cards.example: A monophyletic group is a clade.

cards.front: What is a shared derived character?
cards.back: A trait state originating in a common ancestor and shared by its descendants relative to a comparison group.
cards.example: Such traits help infer clades.

cards.back: A related lineage outside the focal group used for comparison in phylogenetic analysis.
cards.example: An outgroup can help infer ancestral character states.

cards.back: Reciprocal evolutionary change in interacting lineages.
cards.example: Changes in a host can select for changes in its parasite.

cards.back: The loss of every living member of a species or lineage.
cards.example: A lineage ends when no reproducing members remain.

cards.back: The study of interactions among organisms and their environments.
cards.example: Ecologists investigate food webs and resource use.

cards.back: All the interacting populations of different species in an area.
cards.example: A pond community includes algae, insects, and fish.

cards.back: A community together with its physical environment and their interactions.
cards.example: A forest ecosystem includes organisms, soil, water, and energy flows.

cards.back: A broad ecological region characterized by climate and typical vegetation or communities.
cards.example: Tropical rain forest is a terrestrial biome.

cards.back: A species' resource use, environmental requirements, and functional relationships.
cards.example: Two species may differ in feeding time and food choice.

cards.back: The place or environment in which an organism lives.
cards.example: A stream bed is habitat for some insect larvae.

cards.back: The population size an environment can sustain under specified conditions.
cards.example: Resource changes can alter carrying capacity.

cards.back: Growth at a constant per-capita rate under idealized unlimited conditions, producing a J-shaped trajectory.
cards.example: The model is dN/dt = rN.

cards.back: A model in which per-capita growth decreases as population size approaches carrying capacity.
cards.example: The model is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K).

cards.back: A factor whose effect on per-capita population growth depends on population density.
cards.example: Competition often intensifies as density rises.

cards.back: A factor whose per-capita effect is not determined by population density in the model being used.
cards.example: A severe freeze can affect populations regardless of crowding.

cards.back: An interaction in which organisms reduce each other's access to a limiting resource.
cards.example: Plants compete for light.

cards.back: The principle that species with identical limiting-resource niches cannot coexist indefinitely under stable conditions.
cards.example: One competitor may displace another from a shared resource.

cards.back: Differentiation in resource use that reduces competition.
cards.example: Bird species can forage at different heights in one tree.

cards.back: An interaction in which one organism kills and consumes another.
cards.example: An owl eats a mouse.

cards.back: Consumption of plant or algal tissue by an animal.
cards.example: A caterpillar eats leaves.

cards.back: An interaction in which a parasite benefits while harming its host.
cards.example: A tick obtains resources from a mammal.

cards.back: An interaction that benefits both partners under the specified conditions.
cards.example: Mycorrhizal fungi and plants often exchange nutrients beneficially.

cards.back: An interaction benefiting one partner with no substantial effect on the other.
cards.example: An epiphyte may gain support without substantially affecting its host tree.

cards.back: A species with effects on community structure disproportionate to its abundance.
cards.example: A predator can prevent one competitor from dominating.

cards.back: A feeding position in the transfer of energy through a food chain or web.
cards.example: Primary consumers feed on producers.

cards.back: The rate at which autotrophs convert inorganic carbon into organic material.
cards.example: Photosynthetic organisms contribute to primary production.

cards.back: Gross primary production minus the producers' respiratory use of energy or fixed carbon.
cards.example: NPP represents production available for growth and consumers.

cards.back: An organism that breaks down dead organic material and recycles nutrients.
cards.example: Many fungi decompose fallen leaves.

cards.back: Change in community composition over time, often following disturbance or new habitat formation.
cards.example: Plant communities develop on newly exposed surfaces.

cards.back: Increasing concentration of certain persistent substances at higher trophic levels.
cards.example: A persistent contaminant can accumulate strongly in top predators.

cards.back: Nutrient enrichment that can stimulate excessive production and subsequent oxygen depletion.
cards.example: Nutrient runoff can promote an algal bloom.

cards.back: The variety of life, including genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity.
cards.example: A diverse ecosystem can contain many species and genetic variants.

cards.back: A nonnative organism whose introduction and spread cause harm in the receiving environment.
cards.example: An introduced competitor may displace native species.
